unit_name: Britain: Health and the People, c1000 to the present

teaching_brief.what_this_unit_is: A thematic study tracking how medicine, surgery and public health changed in Britain across roughly 1,000 years — medieval (c1000-c1500), Renaissance and early modern (c1500-c1750), industrial and Victorian (c1750-c1900), and modern (c1900-present). The seven AQA factors (war, religion/superstition, chance, government, communication, science and technology, the role of the individual) thread through every period and underpin the 16-mark factor essay that dominates the paper.
teaching_brief.what_is_assessed_overall: Paper 2 Section A is 40 marks of the GCSE total. Within this option students answer a fixed sequence of question types: a 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' between two periods, an 8-mark 'Explain Significance' on a named individual or development, an 8-mark 'Explain a Development', and a 16-mark 'Factors Essay' that names one factor and asks students to weigh it against others. The factor essay carries 40% of the option's marks and is the single highest-leverage skill in the unit.
core_narratives_students_must_master: Continuity then collapse: Galenic-Hippocratic medicine and the four humours dominated medieval Britain and only began to crack in the Renaissance — Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s-90s) and Harvey (1628) corrected Galen on anatomy, surgery and circulation but did not change everyday practice for over a century.

Religion as both engine and brake: monasteries spread literacy, hospitals and care; Islamic medicine preserved Galen and added new ideas (Al-Razi, Ibn Sina); the Church then prevented dissection and treated disease as divine punishment, slowing change. Religion is therefore a factor that pushes both ways across the sweep.

Two leaps in disease theory: Jenner's vaccination (1796) was empirical but theory-free — he could not explain why cowpox prevented smallpox. Pasteur's germ theory (1860s) and Koch's microbe-hunting (1870s-80s) gave Lister the basis for antiseptic surgery (1867) and finally toppled miasma theory.

Public health, from individual responsibility to state duty: cholera epidemics (1831, 1848, 1854), Snow's Broad Street pump (1854), Chadwick's 1842 report, and the 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts trace the shift from laissez-faire to compulsory government action.

From Liberal reforms to NHS: Booth and Rowntree's poverty studies, Boer War recruitment shock, the 1906-11 Liberal reforms, two world wars, the 1942 Beveridge Report, and Bevan's NHS in 1948 — a single causal chain students must hold together.

Modern challenges: Fleming's penicillin (1928, mass-produced 1940s), DNA and genetic medicine, keyhole surgery, antibiotic resistance, an ageing population, mental health and the cost crisis of 21st-century healthcare.

common_misconceptions.topic: Medieval medicine was 'backward' with no progress
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume nothing useful happened in medicine between c1000 and c1500 because supernatural causes and bleeding patients look ridiculous to modern eyes.
common_misconceptions.correction: Within its own framework medieval medicine made real progress — Islamic hospitals in Baghdad and Damascus were better organised than European ones, Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was a teaching standard for 600 years, herbal remedies often had genuine pharmacological effects, and monastic infirmaries provided structured care. The Black Death exposed the limits of the system but did not stop the system functioning.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner reports on Health and the People; Wellcome Collection Health and the medieval church

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that Vesalius's Fabrica (1543) or Harvey's De Motu Cordis (1628) immediately transformed medical practice in Britain.
common_misconceptions.correction: Both corrected Galen on anatomy and physiology but the impact on actual treatment was minimal for at least a century — Galenic teaching dominated universities, and it took until the 19th century for circulation theory to feed into clinical care via blood transfusions. The lesson here is the gap between discovery and application.
common_misconceptions.source: Britannica articles on Vesalius and Harvey; AQA mark scheme commentary on significance questions

common_misconceptions.topic: Germ theory and antiseptics happened simultaneously
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate Pasteur's discovery (germ theory, published 1861) with practical application (Lister's antiseptic surgery, 1867 onwards) and assume germs were universally accepted by the 1870s.
common_misconceptions.correction: Pasteur proved germs caused fermentation in the 1860s; Lister applied this to surgery from 1865 and published in The Lancet in 1867; many British surgeons rejected antiseptics until the 1880s because they could not see germs and found carbolic acid spray cumbersome. Koch's identification of specific bacteria (1876 anthrax, 1882 TB) is what finally settled the question.
common_misconceptions.source: Science Museum on Lister's antisepsis system; Britannica on germ theory

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the NHS in 1948 as a feel-good consensus moment.
common_misconceptions.correction: The British Medical Association told members to refuse to participate in January 1948 — six months before launch — calling Bevan's plan 'so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely by all practitioners.' Bevan compromised by letting consultants keep private patients and GPs run their own practices ('I stuffed their mouths with gold'). Without that, there would be no NHS.
common_misconceptions.source: The National Archives, The foundation of the NHS

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that every change in medical history is progress, missing the spec's explicit prompt to ask 'whether change brought progress.'
common_misconceptions.correction: Some change was regression (the loss of Roman public health after c450), some was sideways (medieval Christian hospitals replaced classical ones with different functions), some was contested (anti-vaccination movement, 1853 Vaccination Act resistance, NHS-resistant BMA). 'Progress' implies a benchmark — students need to name whose perspective they are judging from.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA spec 8145 4.4.2; AQA examiner reports on factor essays

common_misconceptions.topic: Listing factors instead of weighing the named factor
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer the 16-mark question by writing one paragraph on each factor without ever returning to the named factor in the question.
common_misconceptions.correction: The mark scheme rewards complex sustained judgement on the stated factor relative to others — top-band answers compare directly ('government action mattered more than science here because...') and reach a substantiated overall judgement, not a list.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA mark scheme 8145/2A/A; AQA examiner reports

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat each period in isolation and cannot give examples 'across two time periods' as the 16-mark question requires.
common_misconceptions.correction: Examiner reports flag that strong answers move fluently between periods (e.g. comparing the role of government in 1348, 1848 and 1948) rather than writing four self-contained mini-essays.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A factor essays

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark factor essay must use at least three examples drawn from at least two different time periods, and must keep returning to the named factor — not just listing all seven.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA mark scheme 8145/2A/A specimen and June 2022; AQA examiner commentary

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark significance question rewards both importance at the time and importance over time — answers that only describe the figure's contribution at the moment of discovery cap at the lower mark band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA examiner reports on significance questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' question wants two distinct comparisons — students who write one comparison twice or list features without comparing lose half the marks.

Across the unit, named individuals (Vesalius, Harvey, Paré, Hunter, Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Ehrlich, Simpson, Lister, Snow, Chadwick, Nightingale, Booth, Rowntree, Beveridge, Bevan, Fleming, Florey, Chain) are explicit spec content — vague gestures at 'a scientist' or 'a doctor' are penalised.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec 8145 section 3.4.4 AA Britain: Health and the people

teaching_brief.thematic_factors_anchor: Every lesson should explicitly tag which of the seven AQA factors are at work and how they interact. The final two lessons synthesise these factors across the whole sweep so students can weigh them in the 16-mark essay. Factors: war, superstition and religion, chance, government, communication, science and technology, the role of the individual.

skills_focus_per_question_type.4_marks_two_ways_similar_or_different: Compare two specific developments across periods (e.g. medieval and modern hospitals; Jenner's vaccination and modern vaccination programmes). Two distinct comparisons, one sentence each, with a concrete example for each.
skills_focus_per_question_type.8_marks_explain_significance: Pick one named individual or development. Cover both importance at the time (what changed because of them) and importance over time (their legacy across later periods). Two-paragraph structure with linking phrases.
skills_focus_per_question_type.8_marks_explain_a_development: Take a specific development (e.g. 'the development of antiseptic surgery') and explain how and why it occurred. Causal chain — preconditions, trigger, response, consequence — not narrative description.
skills_focus_per_question_type.16_marks_factors_essay: Named factor in the question, weighed against at least two others, with three examples drawn from at least two different periods, reaching a substantiated overall judgement on whether the named factor was the main driver.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Galen
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Theory of the four humours, anatomy and physiology — dominant in medieval Britain and only seriously challenged by Vesalius and Harvey.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hippocrates
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Clinical observation, Hippocratic Corpus, ethical principle — foundational for medieval doctor's training.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Al-Razi (Rhazes) and Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Preserved and extended Galenic medicine; Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles; Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine taught for 600 years.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Andreas Vesalius
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: De Humani Corporis Fabrica — corrected Galen's anatomy through human dissection.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Ambroise Paré
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Replaced cauterisation with ligatures; battlefield surgery; soothing salves.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Harvey
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: De Motu Cordis — circulation of the blood.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Thomas Sydenham
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: 'English Hippocrates' — clinical observation, classification of diseases.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Hunter
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Scientific surgery; teacher of Jenner; experimental method.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edward Jenner
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Vaccination using cowpox to prevent smallpox; opposition from clergy and variolators.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Louis Pasteur
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Germ theory of disease; later vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax, rabies.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Koch
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Specific microbes — anthrax 1876, TB 1882, cholera 1883; staining and culture techniques.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Paul Ehrlich
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Salvarsan 606, the first 'magic bullet' for syphilis.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: James Simpson
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Chloroform anaesthetic; opposition from clergy and surgeons.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Lister
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Carbolic acid antiseptic surgery in Glasgow; published in The Lancet 1867; resistance from older surgeons.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Snow
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Broad Street pump map — proved cholera was waterborne; preceded germ theory.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edwin Chadwick
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population — laid groundwork for 1848 Public Health Act.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Florence Nightingale
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Crimean War nursing; Notes on Nursing 1859; reformed hospital design and nursing as profession.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Charles Booth and Seebohm Rowntree
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Poverty studies in London (Booth) and York (Rowntree) — provided evidence base for Liberal reforms.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: David Lloyd George and the Liberal government
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Old age pensions 1908; National Insurance Act 1911 (sickness and unemployment).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Beveridge
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Beveridge Report — 'five giants' (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness); blueprint for the welfare state.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Aneurin Bevan
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Created the NHS as Minister of Health; faced down BMA opposition through compromise.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Fleming's accidental discovery of penicillin (1928); Florey and Chain mass-produced it for WWII; chance plus science plus war.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: British Medical Association (BMA)
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Initially rejected NHS; deal struck so consultants kept private practice and GPs ran their own surgeries.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Christian Church and monasteries
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Built and ran hospitals; preserved classical texts; restricted dissection; framed disease as divine punishment.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Islamic scholars and Bimaristans
key_individuals_and_groups.contribution: Hospitals in Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo; pharmacology; surgical instruments; teaching texts that returned to Europe via Spain.

lessons.title: Medieval Medicine: Humours, Galen and the Doctor's World
lessons.description: How Galenic theory and the four humours shaped diagnosis and training in medieval Britain c1000-1500.
lessons.spec_anchor: Medieval medicine: approaches including natural, supernatural, ideas of Hippocratic and Galenic methods and treatments; the medieval doctor; training, beliefs about cause of illness.
key_content: Hippocratic clinical observation and the Hippocratic Corpus
Galen's four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) and the theory of opposites
Natural vs supernatural explanations of disease (miasma, sin, astrology, imbalance)
Training of medieval doctors at Salerno, Bologna, Oxford — book-learning over dissection
Diagnosis: urine charts, pulse, zodiac man, humoural matching
Why Galen survived: fit with Christian view of the divinely-ordered body, taught from Latin texts, no rival framework
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Describing the medieval doctor's worldview accurately for 8-mark significance and development questions on later figures who challenged it.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That medieval doctors were 'stupid' — they were operating coherently within a framework where humoural balance made sense; the issue was the framework itself was wrong, not their reasoning.

lessons.title: The Church, the Monastery and Islamic Medicine
lessons.description: How Christianity and Islam between them preserved, spread and shaped medieval medical practice.
lessons.spec_anchor: Medical progress: the contribution of Christianity to medical progress and treatment; hospitals; the nature and importance of Islamic medicine and surgery; surgery in medieval times, ideas and techniques.
key_content: Monastic infirmaries — clean water, herb gardens, structured care; St Bartholomew's 1123, St Thomas's 1173
The Church as both engine (literacy, preserving texts, charitable hospitals) and brake (banning dissection 1163, framing disease as sin)
Islamic Golden Age: Bimaristans, Al-Razi distinguishing smallpox from measles, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
Surgery in medieval times: cauterisation, trepanning, bonesetting, John of Arderne's fistula treatment, anaesthetic 'dwale'
How Islamic medicine returned to Europe via Toledo and Salerno translations
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Religion as a factor that pushed both ways — strong material for the 16-mark factor essay when 'superstition and religion' is the named factor.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the Church only held medicine back. It also funded hospitals, preserved texts and produced trained practitioners; without monastic copying, Galen would have been lost.

lessons.title: Public Health in the Middle Ages and the Black Death
lessons.description: Towns, monasteries and the catastrophe of 1348 — beliefs, treatments and the limits of medieval public health.
lessons.spec_anchor: Public health in the Middle Ages: towns and monasteries; the Black Death in Britain, beliefs about its causes, treatment and prevention.
key_content: Public health in medieval towns — cesspits, rakers, butchery rules; vs monastic plumbing and reredorters
The Black Death arrives in Britain 1348 — bubonic and pneumonic plague
Beliefs about cause: God's punishment, miasma, planetary alignment, Jews (in Europe), foreigners
Treatments: prayer, processions, flagellation, herbal remedies, bleeding, posies of flowers
Prevention: quarantine in some towns, 1348 Royal proclamation cleaning London streets, fleeing the city
Aftermath: depopulation, Statute of Labourers 1351, Peasants' Revolt 1381, gradual change to wages and land
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' question on the response to the Black Death — causal chain not narrative.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That medieval people did nothing — quarantine, cleaning streets, isolating the sick all happened, just without an effective theoretical basis.

lessons.title: Renaissance Anatomy: Vesalius, Paré and the Challenge to Galen
lessons.description: How human dissection and battlefield surgery began to crack Galen's authority in the 16th century.
lessons.spec_anchor: The impact of the Renaissance on Britain: challenge to medical authority in anatomy, physiology and surgery; the work of Vesalius, Paré, William Harvey; opposition to change.
key_content: The Renaissance context: humanism, printing press, return to original Greek texts, Reformation weakens Church monopoly
Vesalius at Padua: De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543) — corrected over 200 of Galen's anatomical errors
Ambroise Paré on the battlefield (1530s-1590s) — replaced boiling oil with soothing salve (chance discovery), used ligatures instead of cauterisation
Why uptake was slow in Britain: Galen still taught at universities, English language editions of Vesalius rare, no immediate change in treatment
Opposition: Vesalius accused of heresy, Paré ridiculed by Paris faculty
Communication factor: printing press multiplied effect of new ideas
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Vesalius or Paré — must cover both 'at the time' (their direct corrections) and 'over time' (foundation for later anatomy and surgery).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Vesalius 'changed medicine' — his book changed anatomical knowledge but routine treatment continued on Galenic lines for over a century.

lessons.title: Harvey, Sydenham and Disease Treatment c1600-1750
lessons.description: Circulation, observation and the slow modernisation of physic — quackery, plague and a new clinical method.
lessons.spec_anchor: Dealing with disease: traditional and new methods of treatments; quackery; methods of treating disease; plague; the growth of hospitals; changes to the training and status of surgeons and physicians; the work of John Hunter.
key_content: William Harvey, De Motu Cordis (1628) — proved the heart pumps blood in a circulation, overturned Galen on liver-as-source
Thomas Sydenham, the 'English Hippocrates' — clinical observation, classifying diseases (smallpox, scarlet fever, gout)
Quackery and patent medicines — Daffy's Elixir, James's Powder; how communication (newspapers) spread them
The Great Plague of London (1665) — quarantine, plague doctors, no theoretical advance on 1348
Voluntary hospitals 1700s — Westminster (1719), Guy's (1724), London (1740) — change in scale not yet in theory
John Hunter (late 18th c) — scientific surgery, dissection-based teaching, taught Jenner
Surgeons separate from barbers (1745); physicians still elite, surgeons still trade
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 4-mark 'Two Ways Similar or Different' between medieval and 18th-century hospitals or doctors.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Harvey's circulation discovery transformed treatment — it took until 1818 (Blundell, first human-to-human transfusion) and beyond before circulation theory yielded clinical applications.

lessons.title: Jenner, Vaccination and the Limits of 18th-Century Prevention
lessons.description: How a country doctor's chance observation produced vaccination — and why it was fiercely opposed.
lessons.spec_anchor: Prevention of disease: inoculation; Edward Jenner, vaccination and opposition to change.
key_content: Inoculation (variolation) — imported from Turkey by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu c1721; risky but reduced smallpox mortality
Jenner's Gloucestershire observation: milkmaids who had cowpox did not catch smallpox
1796 experiment on James Phipps; published Inquiry 1798
Why this was different: empirical, theory-free — Jenner could not explain WHY it worked, which fed opposition
Opposition: variolators (commercial loss), clergy (transferring 'beast matter' to humans, satirised in Gillray's 1802 cartoon), some doctors
Government response: 1802 grant £10,000, 1807 grant £20,000; 1853 Vaccination Act made it compulsory; 1898 conscience clause after riots
Significance over time: Pasteur extended the principle in 1880s; smallpox eradicated 1980 (WHO)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Jenner — at the time (saved thousands) and over time (template for later vaccines, government role in compulsory health).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Jenner discovered germ theory. He did not — vaccination worked but its mechanism was a black box for over 60 years until Pasteur.

lessons.title: Pasteur, Koch and the Germ Theory Revolution
lessons.description: How germ theory replaced miasma — and how scepticism in Britain delayed practical change.
lessons.spec_anchor: The development of Germ Theory and its impact on the treatment of disease in Britain: the importance of Pasteur, Robert Koch and microbe hunting; Pasteur and vaccination; Paul Ehrlich and magic bullets; everyday medical treatments and remedies.
key_content: Miasma theory dominant up to mid-19th century — bad air causes disease
Pasteur 1861 Germ Theory of Disease — published after work on fermentation for the brewing industry
Koch's microbe hunting: anthrax 1876, staining technique, agar-jelly culture; TB 1882; cholera 1883
Pasteur extends his vaccine principle: chicken cholera 1879 (chance — old culture left over holiday), anthrax 1881, rabies 1885
Paul Ehrlich, Salvarsan 606 (1909) — first 'magic bullet' for syphilis; Prontosil (1932) for streptococcal infection
British scepticism: many doctors trained on miasma; germ theory only filtered into NHS-era textbooks slowly
Communication factor: Pasteur and Koch competed publicly, German-French scientific rivalry drove output
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay practice — was 'science and technology' the main factor in understanding disease? Pasteur and Koch as your central case.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That germ theory was instantly accepted. Many British surgeons and public health officials clung to miasma into the 1880s.

lessons.title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics
lessons.description: How chloroform and carbolic acid moved surgery from butchery to safety — and why opposition slowed the change.
lessons.spec_anchor: A revolution in surgery: anaesthetics, including Simpson and chloroform; antiseptics, including Lister and carbolic acid; surgical procedures; aseptic surgery.
key_content: Pre-anaesthetic surgery: speed (Liston amputating in 28 seconds), high mortality, restricted to crisis cases
Nitrous oxide (Davy 1799), ether (Morton, Boston 1846), chloroform (Simpson, Edinburgh 1847)
Opposition to chloroform: clergy citing Genesis 'in sorrow shalt thou bring forth'; surgeons fearing patients died from anaesthetic; resolved partly by Queen Victoria's use in 1853 for Prince Leopold
The 'Black Period' 1846-1865 — anaesthetics encouraged longer, deeper surgery but infection killed 50% of patients
Lister 1865 reads Pasteur, applies carbolic acid in Glasgow; publishes The Lancet 1867
Resistance to Lister: spray was unpleasant, surgeons could not see germs, results variable; takes until 1880s to win consensus
Aseptic surgery (sterile environment, rubber gloves Halsted 1894) replaces antiseptic by 1900
WWI as accelerator — blood transfusions, X-rays (Röntgen 1895), shrapnel surgery
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' on the development of antiseptic surgery — clear causal chain (germ theory + Listers reading + carbolic acid + falling mortality + uptake).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That anaesthetics solved surgery. They actually made the infection problem worse before Lister solved it.

lessons.title: Public Health in the Industrial City: Snow, Chadwick and the Acts
lessons.description: Cholera, the Broad Street pump and the long road from the 1848 Act to the 1875 Act.
lessons.spec_anchor: Improvements in public health: public health problems in industrial Britain; cholera epidemics; the role of public health reformers; local and national government involvement in public health improvement, including the 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts.
key_content: Industrial Britain: rapid urbanisation, back-to-backs, no sewers, Whig laissez-faire opposition to state action
Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) — argued bad housing caused poverty not the reverse
1848 Public Health Act — General Board of Health, but adoptive (towns chose to opt in) and limited
John Snow 1854 — Broad Street pump map; removed handle; convinced local officials but not the medical establishment
Joseph Bazalgette's London sewers 1865 — built in response to the 1858 'Great Stink', validated by 1866 cholera not reaching sewered districts
1875 Public Health Act (Disraeli, after 1867 working-class franchise) — compulsory, comprehensive; Artisans' Dwellings Act same year
Why the shift? Government factor combines with science (Snow), communication (Punch cartoons, Mayhew's London Labour), and chance (Great Stink forcing Parliament to act)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay — was government the main factor in improving public health? Compare 1848 to 1875.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the 1848 Act fixed public health. It barely worked because it was adoptive and short-lived; the 1875 Act, after wider voting rights and germ theory, was the real shift.

lessons.title: Nightingale, Hospitals and the Reform of Nursing
lessons.description: How war, statistics and a determined individual transformed Victorian hospitals and the nursing profession.
lessons.spec_anchor: Improvements in public health (cont.); changes to the training and status of surgeons and physicians (linked); growth of hospitals.
key_content: Pre-Crimean nursing: untrained, often drunk, low status (Dickens's Sairey Gamp)
Crimean War 1854-56: Nightingale and 38 nurses to Scutari; mortality fell from ~42% to ~2% in six months
Nightingale used statistics — pioneered the rose diagram (polar area chart) to convince Parliament
Notes on Nursing (1859) and Notes on Hospitals (1859); Nightingale Training School at St Thomas's 1860
Pavilion-plan hospitals — long wards, ventilation, separation by disease
Mary Seacole — Crimean nurse, refused by War Office, ran 'British Hotel' near front; recognition delayed until late 20th century
Linked spec content: status of surgeons and physicians, growth of hospitals — both shift towards professional, regulated bodies (1858 Medical Act)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark significance of Nightingale — at the time (Crimean mortality, lobbying) and over time (professional nursing, hospital design legacy).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Nightingale single-handedly invented nursing. Catholic nursing orders pre-existed her; her achievement was making secular nursing a respected profession in Britain.

lessons.title: From Booth and Rowntree to the Liberal Reforms 1900-1914
lessons.description: How poverty surveys, the Boer War and a Liberal landslide put the state into welfare for the first time.
lessons.spec_anchor: The importance of Booth, Rowntree, and the Boer War; the Liberal social reforms.
key_content: Charles Booth, Life and Labour of the People in London (1889-1903) — 30% of Londoners below the poverty line
Seebohm Rowntree, Poverty: A Study of Town Life (1901) — 28% of York similar; 'primary' (insufficient income) vs 'secondary' poverty
Boer War 1899-1902: 40% of recruits in industrial cities rejected as unfit; national efficiency panic
1906 Liberal landslide — Campbell-Bannerman, then Asquith; pressure from Lloyd George, Churchill (then Liberal), Beveridge (civil servant)
Reforms: Free school meals (1906), School medical inspections (1907), Old Age Pensions Act (1908, means-tested, over 70), Labour Exchanges (1909), People's Budget (1909, Lords crisis)
National Insurance Act 1911 — Part I health insurance for workers (4d worker, 3d employer, 2d state, 'ninepence for fourpence'), Part II unemployment insurance for select trades
Limits: contributory not universal; wives and children mostly excluded; opposition from BMA, Labour, friendly societies
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 8-mark 'Explain a Development' on the Liberal reforms — preconditions (Booth, Rowntree, Boer War), trigger (1906 election), response (Acts), consequences (basis for later welfare state).
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the Liberal reforms were the welfare state. They were a partial, contributory, work-tested step — universal welfare waited for Beveridge and Bevan.

lessons.title: Penicillin, Modern Surgery and the Wars
lessons.description: How chance, individuals and the demands of two world wars produced the antibiotic age and modern surgery.
lessons.spec_anchor: Modern treatment of disease: the development of the pharmaceutical industry; penicillin, its discovery by Fleming, its development; new diseases and treatments, antibiotic resistance; alternative treatments. The impact of war and technology on surgery: plastic surgery; blood transfusions; X-rays; transplant surgery; modern surgical methods, including lasers, radiation therapy and keyhole surgery.
key_content: Fleming 1928 — chance contamination of staphylococcus plate by Penicillium notatum; published 1929 but moved on
Florey and Chain at Oxford from 1939 — purified penicillin, mouse experiment 1940, first human patient 1941 (PC Albert Alexander, died when supply ran out)
WWII brought US mass-production from 1941 — by D-Day 1944, enough for all Allied wounded; Nobel Prize 1945
Plastic surgery: Harold Gillies WWI (Queen's Hospital Sidcup); Archibald McIndoe WWII Guinea Pig Club at East Grinstead
Blood transfusions: Landsteiner blood groups 1901; WWI storage advances; National Blood Transfusion Service 1946
X-rays: Röntgen 1895; rapid wartime adoption from 1914
Modern surgery: keyhole (laparoscopic) from 1980s; transplants — Christiaan Barnard heart 1967; lasers; radiotherapy
Antibiotic resistance: MRSA from 1960s; rising public health concern from 1990s
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay — was 'chance' the main factor in modern medicine? Fleming's mould plus Pasteur's chicken cholera plus Paré's salve as a sweep across periods.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That Fleming created penicillin as a working drug. He saw the effect; Florey and Chain made it a medicine; war forced mass production.

lessons.title: Beveridge, Bevan and the Birth of the NHS
lessons.description: How the 1942 Beveridge Report and a Labour government created universal healthcare in 1948 — and the fights to get there.
lessons.spec_anchor: Modern public health: the impact of two world wars on public health, poverty and housing; the Beveridge Report and the Welfare State; creation and development of the National Health Service; costs, choices and the issues of healthcare in the 21st century.
key_content: WWII context: evacuation exposed urban poverty to rural Britain; rationing improved working-class diet; Emergency Medical Service nationalised hospitals temporarily
Beveridge Report December 1942 — five 'giants on the road to reconstruction': want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness
300,000 copies sold; popular pressure made post-war welfare politically unavoidable
1945 Labour landslide — Attlee government, Bevan as Minister of Health
NHS Act 1946 passed; opposition from Conservatives in Parliament and the BMA in the medical press
BMA January 1948: 'so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely'
Bevan's compromise: consultants kept private patients ('I stuffed their mouths with gold'); GPs ran their own practices as contractors not employees
5 July 1948 — NHS opens; free at point of use, funded by taxation; first universal system in the world
Other welfare state Acts 1944-48: Education Act 1944, Family Allowances 1945, National Insurance Act 1946, National Assistance Act 1948
lessons.exam_skill_focus: 16-mark factor essay practice — was war the main factor in creating the NHS? WWII context vs Beveridge as individual vs Labour government.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the NHS was a national consensus. Bevan won by political calculation against active medical opposition; the deal had explicit costs (private practice survives inside the NHS).

lessons.title: Weighing the Factors: Continuity, Change and Progress c1000-Today
lessons.description: Synthesising the seven factors across a thousand years to write a top-band 16-mark factor essay.
lessons.spec_anchor: All four parts; explicit synthesis lesson on the seven factors and the rate, direction and meaning of change.
key_content: Mapping the seven factors against the four spec parts — which factor dominates in which period?

The 16-mark factor essay structure: introduction (define factor + judgement), factor paragraph (named factor with two periods of evidence), counter-factor paragraphs (at least two other factors), conclusion (substantiated overall judgement)

Worked example: 'Has government been the main factor in improving public health? Explain your answer with reference to government and other factors.' — 1348 (almost no government), 1848 (weak), 1875 (strong), 1948 (decisive); compare to science and individuals
Tackling the change-vs-progress problem: not all change is progress (loss of Roman public health); progress depends on whose perspective
Tackling rate of change: medieval slow, Renaissance start-stop, 19th-century acceleration, 20th-century rapid
21st-century issues: NHS funding, ageing population, antibiotic resistance, mental health, COVID-19 pandemic — students should be able to extend the story to today
Examiner red flags: writing in first person, listing factors without judgement, using only one period, vague figures (the AQA examiner reports flag this every series)
lessons.exam_skill_focus: Whole-paper rehearsal — 4-mark, 8-mark significance, 8-mark development and 16-mark factors essay all modelled in this lesson with the seven factors as the spine.
lessons.misconception_to_address: That the 16-mark question is about cramming all seven factors. It is about weighing the named factor against two or three carefully chosen others, with three examples across at least two periods, and reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
